utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you. Can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Yes. I can hear you in a language I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Joanna Korner, Anna Richterova, Ann Sutherland, assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm John Ackerman, with David Cunningham and Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you, Mr. Ackerman. Good morning to you too. So before we bring in the witness, I understand two things. First of all, Mr. Ackerman, you would like to be excused this morning. I take it that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just feeling very poorly. I don't think I can go forward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Mr. Sebire we will have to make arrangements to have Mr. Sebire back. I don't know when. Second thing: Yesterday, and this is rendering an account of what happened in my chambers. Yesterday we had what was supposed to be a very frank and -- frank discussion between Chamber and lawyers, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, as to when the Prosecution should be in a position or should be expected to finish its case, and also to give an indication of roughly the time frame needed to enable this Trial Chamber to finish and hand down its final decision, judgement, before the end of August of next year, 2004. During the hearing, also, or during the meeting also I made the Chamber available for what would be the second day of the plenary, that is, Friday, the 18th of July, assuming that plenary would probably be finished by then, and we also offered to sit on Friday, the 1st August, when we were not scheduled to sit. We also conceded that the maximum that we could go at the time was until Friday, the 29th of August, considering, in particular, that I was supposed to be away from The Hague and away from this Tribunal in the course of the week commencing on the 21st of July until the 25th of July, both days included. This was taken into account in the course of the discussion. I also explained why my absence -- what was behind my expected absence from The Hague, and I also invited the parties, if it was at all possible, to go through the tentative schedule that we had prepared, to see whether this would be -- would necessitate any amendments. It came to my knowledge this morning that Ms. Korner, behind our back, having had the opportunity to express her disagreement or discontent with the fact that we were not sitting on -- between the 21st and the 25th of July, and without even mentioning that she would have had a problem, because these witnesses had already been scheduled to the -- the witnesses scheduled for that particular week were scheduled to come over, even if we are talking of more than a month and a half away from now. As I said, behind our back, went to the President or contacted the President of this Tribunal, complaining about this. This is something which I personally deplore. I am not used to such kind of dealings by any lawyer that I have ever encountered in my career, Ms. Korner, and I want to put this on record. In the meantime, I think most of the discussion that went on between us yesterday does not hold any further, and the Prosecution will be required to finish its -- will be required - I'm sorry, I am in charge of this trial - will be required to finish its case by not later than Friday the 1st day of August, and we will issue a Scheduling Order in due course. In the meantime, you are informed that we will be sitting in the week starting 21st of July, ending 25th of July, both days included. Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry that you feel that I didn't express my discontent in the meeting, because I rather felt that I expressed my discontent very strongly indeed, and we had a discussion, as Your Honour may recall, about whether it was possible for the ad litem Judges to sit in your absence. And no decision had been made, but you made it very clear, as I recall, that if that was possible, that we could not call the scheduled witnesses for that week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you didn't say that you couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we looked at it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I'm going to cut it short, because I'm not used to these kind of dealings, as I said. My career has been conducted as a Judge and as a lawyer on fair play and honest dealings and I do not consider what you did as becoming conduct. So I deplore it in public and I hope it will not happen again, and you will have until Friday the 1st of August to conclude the Prosecution's case, and the case is over. Let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As Your Honour is making this a public reprimand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm making it a public reprimand. No lawyer should go behind the Judge's back to the President without having first expressed his discontent to the Judge. Had you aired this yesterday in the course of the meeting, we would have possibly discussed other matters and other things and other solutions. But you didn't. Instead you chose to do what you have done in the past because I know of other instances where behind my back you went to complain.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I made my -- I'm sorry but you must allow me to at least put this on the record. That I made my discontent very clear and if Your Honour thinks about it and Your Honours' colleagues during the course of that meeting, Your Honour made it clear this is what you proposed to do and I could see no other option but to raise the matter with the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, there were two things that were said yesterday. First, that if these witnesses were going to be brought during the week of the 21st to the 25th of July, then I would have preferred to be presiding rather than be absent. That's number one. And at no time did you say that it was not possible to -- not to bring these witnesses at some other time. That was not even hinted at. And we're talking of a month and a half. Today is the 11th. And we're talking of the 21st to the 25th. And that's it. Let's bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is one other matter, because that may depend on what action we take. Your Honour says we have to finish our case by the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Does that take into account the fact that clearly, and we all understand the reasons why, that Mr. Ackerman may not be able to -- we will be calling all the witnesses that we've listed, but that Mr. Ackerman may not be able to be in a position to cross-examine? Because if that's the case, and time isn't allowed for that, well, then, Your Honour, that would be an unfair proceeding. And it's just not -- it's not me. It's those witnesses the people whom you represent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, that is a problem that we will deal with as we go along. I hope that Mr. Ackerman will not become an accomplice in this, because already I was rather unhappy when all of a sudden you both agreed to extend the end of the Prosecution until the last week of August. I mean, that sounded to me very convenient. I'm not accusing anyone, but I'm making it very clear that the case of the Prosecution must finish by the end of this month -- of next month, 1st August. Mr. Ackerman and Mr. Cunningham will make their utmost to be able to cross-examine the witnesses. In addition, may I suggest to you that you do indeed perhaps think about opting for the procedure that I suggested to you last time, particularly with regard to certain witnesses, in other words, bringing forward the statement, tendering it an exhibit, asking the witness a few questions on the statement, and as additional information that may arise, and then we pass on to the Defence. In this manner, we could actually sit four days a week, as I said yesterday, which would give Mr. Ackerman Friday, Saturday, and Sunday off each week in order to be able to prepare the cross-examination for the following week.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's why I raised this, because if Your Honour is saying that we have to finish the case by the 1st of August, then we would want to sit all the days available. That's why I'm saying, realistically we can do it, but only if we sit the allotted days and only if everything proceeds smoothly. We will keep our witnesses to the estimates that we have given on that list, but that is -- in the sense of in chief, but we are also taking into account that cross-examination will follow and that there will be no days off. Your Honour, I agree this is something we can see as goes along but I'm merely mentioning it at this stage because if Your Honour's ruling was immovable and unchangeable, despite any delays that there may have to be, well then Your Honour clearly it's a matter we will have to consider.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, consider it. And you have considered it in the past in other cases and you got your reply. So -- and probably you will get the same reply in this case. So let's start with the next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not sure whether the witness is here, because Mr. Sebire was scheduled, and I asked to bring the other witness later. But the witness mentioned at the end of sitting with him yesterday that he would like to request protective measures, pseudonym and facial distortion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He had none; no?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He has none at this moment. He told me that he is -- can we go into private session for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have already noticed that I did not address you by your name, and that leads me straight away to informing you of what perhaps is most important for you at this point in time, namely, that the Prosecution asked for, on your behalf, and was granted, protective measures, as far as you are concerned, one being that you will not be referred to by your name but by a nom de plume, by a pseudonym, and you will be referred to here by BT96, in other words, your name will not appear anywhere in the records, for public purposes. And in addition, the Prosecution asked for and was granted what is referred to as facial distortion. In other words, the usher will explain to you, if the cameras are focused on you and you are put on video mode, this is how others will see you. In other words, no one should be able to see your face, and this is by way of trying to do our utmost to protect your identity as you desire, as you wish. Having said that, the usher, who is standing next to you, is going to give you a piece of paper. It contains the text of a solemn declaration that you are required to make by our Rules. It's equivalent to an oath. And basically, what is amounts to is a solemn declaration that in the course of your testimony you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. So I invite you to read that statement aloud, that solemn declaration aloud, and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please take a seat. Madam Richterova, for the Prosecution, will be asking you a few questions, and she will then be followed by Mr. Cunningham, who is appearing for Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin, who is the accused in this case. Your duty, your obligation and responsibility, as a witness, is to answer each question as fully and as truthfully as you can, and that is irrespective of who is putting the question to you. In other words, irrespective of whether it's coming from the Prosecution or from the Defence. Madam Richterova, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may ask the usher to show the witness a piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Please read it for yourself and just say yes or no whether it is your name.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it to Mr. Cunningham, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This would be Exhibit P2022, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I need to inform Your Honours that this witness had some health problems last night, and I would be -- I would like the testimony to make as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you. I was informed of that as well, and I really appreciate, Madam Richterova, that you are bringing it up, because I had meant to address the witness on it, and it just went straight through my mind, and I forgot about it. Sir, I mean, if you at any time you feel uncomfortable in that chair answering questions because you feel either stressed or tired or you're not feeling well, please just let us know and we'll have a break and do whatever is necessary to make sure that you are okay and that you are not undergoing any undue or unnecessary stressful condition, all right? So any time you would like us to stop, just let us know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will do that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If necessary. It is not for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, you gave a statement to the OTP in the year 1999. Did you have opportunity to read the statement yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the witness please speak up or come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I did have the opportunity to read my statement. Yes, I had the opportunity to read that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is everything correct in that statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, it is, everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I took your advice, and I would like to tender the statement of this witness. I would like to tender it into evidence, under P2023, and it should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] What number are we going to give this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And for the record, we are only talking of the statement to the Office of the Prosecutor, to an investigator of the Prosecution, not the other statement that he also gave to the authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No. I am tendering just the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I imagined that to be so, but I wanted to make it clear for the record, and also for Mr. Cunningham. Is there any objection on your part, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I want to ask you only a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if the witness could be shown the Exhibit P1649. It is the very last document in the Krupa binder. I can assist and -- oh, you have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at this document and tell me: Did you have opportunity to have a look at this document and read this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I saw it and read it yesterday, so the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After reading this document, did you reach any conclusion as who is the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Richterova, before it becomes too late, we need to redact this. The previous paragraph of -- in the transcript, that is, the witness's answer needs to be redacted in its entirety. Entirety, yes. The previous answer, when he says: (Redacted) No, no, because he continues. And what I am saying too needs to be redacted too. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (Redacted)-" so that needs to be redacted, and perhaps you will invite him to answer the same question without making any references to himself, as a result of which he could be then identified. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. If there's going to be a redaction with respect to his answer, we would ask that the part following the comma, (Redacted), would be the part that would be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm going to ask him to answer the question again.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me conduct this. And now we can -- sir, you were asked who the author of this document is. Am I correct in saying that it was Gojko Klickovic? Did you say that, according to you, it's Gojko Klickovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Gojko Klickovic worked in which municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what capacity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The vice-president of the Executive Board of the Municipal Assembly and subsequently the president of the Executive Board of the -- in the municipality. Because the vice-president was killed in a traffic accident, so that the vice-president then took over the duties of the president [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And am I correct in saying that you knew him? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before I read some parts of this document, can you tell us very briefly what were the results of the election? How many seats got SDA and how many seats got SDS?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: The assembly of Bosanska Krupa had 92 [as interpreted] deputies. The SDS, 100 per cent Serb votes in the municipality, and I think it was about 21 seats. The SDA won something about 70. That is, the Bosniak population constituted 73 per cent and the party won close to 90 per cent, that is, four or five members were -- represented the communists and the rest represented the SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will read you one passage from this report. It is in B/C/S version first page, second paragraph, and it is the last sentence. It is also first page in English version. And it says: "In the distribution of power, they had no intention of even considering any other factors, and everything revolved around relative number of inhabitants, according to the 1981 census, which the ratio was 72 percentage Muslims, 26 percentage Serbs, and 2 percentage others. However, such power-sharing with a partner like the SDA did not offer Serbs sufficient guarantees for mere survival." After the election, did you deal -- did SDA deal with SDS with respect to power distribution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Our relations were very correct after the elections, and we implemented the results of the elections in no time at all, because we did not perceive the SDS as an enemy; rather, as our partner in power. And we wanted to get over the transition period, to leave the Communism behind and start the democratic processes, because we wanted to enter Europe as a democratic country. And therefore, there were no problems regarding the implementation, and we even gave the SDS more offices than were due them on the basis of the election results. And I can illustrate this by telling you which offices were assigned to them. Mr. Klickovic became the vice-president of the Executive Board; Mirko Orelj was assigned one of the most important offices in the municipality, and that was town planning; Bozo Pilipovic was assigned the office of National Defence; Mladen Drljaca became the secretary of the municipality; and they were all members of the SDS, that is, its top leadership, and I believe this is quite a telling example.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read another part from this document. It is -- it starts in the bottom of page 1, and it is also the last paragraph on page 1 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It will -- in English version, it will start at the bottom of page 1, and it will continue to page 2. It starts: "In addition to developing ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, please have a look at the same page as you had before, the page -- the first page. Yes, this page. And it is the last paragraph. And I will read slowly: "In addition to developing their own plan to create the Serbian municipality of Krupa within the framework of the Serbian Republic of BH, the representatives of the Serbian people in the joint government were instructed to remain as long as possible within that government, such as it was, and to gradually undermine that rotten structure, which consisted of nothing but Islamic fundamentalism and to buy time for another group of SDS people who were busy organising and arming the Serbian people for the defence of their bare existence." And then it goes on, and the last sentence says: "The work on the project for partitioning Bosanska Krupa municipality and establishing the Serbian municipality of Krupa began in the summer of 1991." My first question with respect to this paragraph is: During the year 1991 and first quarter of the year 1992, did you work -- did Municipal Assembly work together? Did representatives of SDA and SDS work together?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes. We worked together right up until the start of the conflict, that is, until the moment when the municipality of Bosanska Krupa was attacked. The administration was working until the very last moment. It was only on the eve of the attack that Serbs quit the offices. Until that time, everything was in order and worked in accordance with election results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Pause, please. We need to redact this entire paragraph. That's the last paragraph, last answer, given by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can the witness repeat this statement in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And I was going to suggest that. We need to redact that first, and then we go straight into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we need to have an open session, this last part of the statement now. So do I take it that you are absolutely opposed to the claim that you saw on this document and that you oppose, in other words, the claim that Islamic fundamentalism was present? Please answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I oppose this claim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement, you were talking about division of the municipality, about the suggestion of the SDS to divide the municipality. Was the division discussed during Municipal Assembly meetings, or was it discussed just during the inter-party meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Only at meetings between two parties, because they were the leading parties, and what they decided among themselves is what the Assembly would also decide.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, was the division of municipality approved by the Municipal Assembly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: The Municipal Assembly never approved this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to direct your attention to the continuation of this paragraph, when it gives reasons for partitioning or division of the municipality. First, we have economic reasons, and then political reasons. And I want to ask you about one of these political reasons. The case involving the Branko Copic monument. Branko Copic is a famous writer. What was this case involving the Branko Copic monument? Can you briefly describe what happened and why it was so important that it made the SDS put it on the list of the main reasons for division of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Branko Copic was a writer who belonged to all the people. We all liked him. He was born in a village near Bosanska Krupa. He was a citizen of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa. He would occasionally visit Bosanska Krupa, and everyone, all citizens, all inhabitants, would be glad to see him there, because of his participation in partisan units, his name was a well-known one in Bosanska Krupa and it was used for the names of streets and schools, and we also had a centre called the Branko Copic cultural centre. And a project was being prepared, Branko's village. It was supposed to be a large complex. Naturally, there were monuments of him. So while he was alive, he had been commemorated in Bosanska Krupa. Mr. Miroslav, while he was an official for town planning in the municipality, abused his position and issued an order that in a small park, a bust of Branko Copic should be erected. That park is across the road from the Orthodox church. I believe in acting legally, and I didn't want this order, which was illegal, to be implemented. I requested that it not be implemented, and I requested that this monument not be erected. This problem was also dealt with in Sarajevo. Mr. Krajisnik, who was at the time the president of the municipality, was also -- of the Assembly, the president of the Assembly, was also aware of this. The question was why have a monument applied -- it wasn't a matter of not allowing a monument to be erected. It was a matter of the decision being illegal, and this would open the way to illegal acts. If this had been allowed, it would have opened the way to other illegal acts. The SDA insisted on this being done. The SDS is a political party. We had executive authority and we couldn't allow such an illegal decision to be implemented. They thought that their reputation had been tainted, that they had a legitimate request, and that we acted out of spite. But it was a matter of a decision which was illegal, decision for a monument to be erected. I don't know why --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time that you feel that we should go into private session, please let me know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned this Mr. Miroslav. What was his full name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Miroslav Vjestica. He was an administrative official. He later left that position and became a professor. He was the SDS member and he became a professional member of the SDS. He was a key member in this party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to ask you about one more thing from these political reasons, and it is purchase of Serbian staff from the high school centre, the social services centre, Municipal Assembly organs, the municipal library, the media. Were the Serbs fired from their positions during the period of 1991, 19 -- the first quarter of 1993? I'm sorry. The first quarter of 1992.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No, the Serbs weren't fired from their positions. Some changes were made of key figures at certain positions, not because certain individuals were Serbs or weren't Serbs. But people who were part of the former regime were being replaced. The people who had been appointed by the Communist Party, the central committee, these people were replaced. Although it was also necessary to establish a balance among the leading figures, because in the former system, the Serbs had the majority. I'll just provide you one example. There were 23 per cent of Serbs in this municipality, and the number of Serbs in the police force was over 60 per cent, and that concerns leading positions -- an ordinary policeman. The chief of police was a Serb, and only the fifth person in the chain of command was a Muslim. So for the sake of our political authenticities, the SDA party, we had to attempt to improve this ratio which was in favour of the Serbs. I want to say that no one was dismissed because he was a Serb. He could be dismissed from a key position, but this person would remain employed, in accordance with -- or according to that person's professional capacity and according to that person's knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I have now last question with respect to this document. If you could have a look on page two in B/C/S version, last paragraph. And in English version, it is page 4, and the first full paragraph. It says: "The negotiations began on 16 January 1992 and gave no promise of a peaceful outcome, because the initial position of the Serbian delegation was that we can talk about everything, but about life together never again." You already mentioned that there were negotiations -- did you find this paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, I found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There were negotiations between parties, and I understand that you will probably not remember any specific dates. But what I just read, we can talk about everything but not about life together," was this the position of the SDS during the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes. That was the SDS's position in the course of the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I have now the last question. Did you know or did you get aware of Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin in due course of 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I didn't know him personally, but I knew about him from the press and from the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What did you know about him? Did you see him on television?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I knew that he was an important figure in the SDS. He acted in a fairly authoritative manner. I think he was also a representative -- a deputy in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know for which -- did he work for the Autonomous Region of Krajina or for Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I knew that he was from Banja Luka, and if someone is from Banja Luka, then his activities relate to that area. I had heard about the Autonomous Region of Krajina, but I didn't have any particular information about that, especially not written information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned that he acted in a fairly authoritative manner. Were you able to see whether people respected him or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, when I say in an authoritative manner, I mean that when he spoke, others would listen to him, and it was on that basis that I came to that conclusion, because there were other speakers to whom people would not listen. He was obviously an important man, and many questions were put to him. People would turn to him with regard to many issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I've concluded my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I pass you on to Mr. Cunningham, who will be cross-examining you, I notice in your statement that you give the name of the commander of police as Lazar Kovacevic, and there is at least two occasions in your statement when you refer to him by that name. Was it Lazar Kovacevic or Lazar Stupar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lazar Stupar.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So for the record, where in the statement we have Lazar Kovacevic, that's a mistake. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Before I start, Judge, Your Honours, because this is the first time I've dealt with a witness where we might have to go into private session, I'm going to be extremely cautious. I hope I don't overstep by bounds, and I trust the Court will tell me that it's time to be out of private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are we going into private session straight away or not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, not yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. I want to talk with you about the last area that you spoke with us about, and that is the defendant, seeing the defendant on TV. You personally have never met him, have you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And we all know what your position was. But in your position, as a citizen of your municipality, did you ever see him in your municipality during 1990, 1991, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I don't remember having seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. You would have -- do you remember reading anything in your local newspaper, anything in your local media, that reported his presence in your municipality, during the time period 1990-1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: He was rarely mentioned in the local media, if you're referring to the local radio. He mostly appeared in the state media.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And it is in the state media during this time period, 1991, 1992, is when you saw him; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And how many times do you think you saw him on TV?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Would you like a number or an estimate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If you can give us a number, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: More than 20 times.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And in your testimony today -- let me back up. Neither in your testimony today nor in your written statements was there any indication that you recalled specifically what he was talking about; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: You're right to the extent that I can't quote anything that he said now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And it is based on what you saw on TV alone that you came to the conclusion that he was authoritative and people respected him; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: It would be correct to say that that is the impression I had gained on the basis of his television appearances, that in the press and in the television, he would represent the SDS's policies, and I could provide additional comments about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't really want the additional comments. I was just wondering what was the basis of your conclusion. So let me move to a new topic, and what I'm going to do is I'm going to go back to the elections. Because in your statement -- and by the way, sir, do you have your written statement that you gave to the OTP available? Do you have your written statement on the witness stand with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to confirm with you, Mr. Witness, that that is indeed your written statement.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Just a minute. This is the English version. It's my authentic statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And I assume that prior to coming inside the courtroom, inside this Tribunal, that you had the opportunity to review that statement. Have you reviewed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, I have had the opportunity of reviewing it. I immediately knew which statement was concerned. I didn't review it very carefully, but I did check to make sure that this is the statement that I made.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you some questions that may require you to refer to your statement. I want you to feel free to refer to that statement if you need to to refresh your recollection. I want to talk briefly with you about the election that you discuss on page 2, and I have it on page 2 of the English version. Because in your statement, you say the following: "The election campaign was very aggressively fought by the SDS, with extensive use of iconography and nationalist symbols." Do you remember making that statement and do you see it in front of you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And if you could, very briefly, tell us what you mean by the use of the nationalist symbols and the icons.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, I meant symbols that we weren't familiar with in the socialist Yugoslavia. I assume that they had been forbidden. It was a coat of arms with a two-headed eagle, and with four S's across, with four letters S, a flag that we had not seen until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Did the SDA have anything similar to that? Did they have any flags or icons that were used in their campaigns?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: The SDA was a political party that represented the majority of the Muslim population, and it didn't have national symbols or religious symbols. It was called the Party of Democratic Action. Its abbreviation was SDA. This was all done in a new democratic environment, and in a way that did not have national characteristics, because our nationality was also a matter of dispute -- had also been a matter of dispute over the course of the last 50 years, since we had all -- we had mainly been reduced to the level of a religious group. We had been treated as a religious group. It was only after the war that we were given the name the Bosniaks, and that was our national designation.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me take you now to after the election, where there are -- and this is going to be my phrase. There's an allocation of positions of authority between the parties. And I'm going to paraphrase you, and I don't mean to try to confuse you in doing this, but basically, my recollection is you said something to the effect that the parties got together and certain seats were given to the SDA and certain positions were given to the SDA [sic]. Am I right? That was negotiated between the two parties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: That is also the political practice now. So yes, you are right. The two leading parties agreed about the assignment of offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: The assignment of offices was something that was reached between the two parties in good faith discussion, in good faith negotiations; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Correct. We did it in good faith and without tongue in cheek.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. In your statement, you talk about how, after the elections, after people were -- the seats had been allocated, the positions of power had been allocated, things were functioning well in the municipality. But then you tell us -- isn't it true that there were certain things that started to happen in the municipality that raised some tension between the Serbs and the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, if I tell you that the municipal budget was adopted, then I think you will accept it as a fact showing that the administration, that the government functioned. Salaries were paid out to the employed, which is another sign of the correct functioning of that administration. The police was organised and worked well. And if you need any more information ...

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No. That's plenty, and I think we can agree that in the wake of the election, everything was going smoothly in the town, but there were some issues that arose between the Serbian population and the government, and one of those was the Branko Copic -- dispute over the monument. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I've explained it already, and I have nothing to change --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: -- in my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'm not trying to get you to change anything, but what I'm trying to find out is: That was an area of at least discussion between the SDA in control in the Serbian population; that was an issue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Between the SDA and the Serb population? No. That was not an issue. The SDS misused Copic and tried to use him for its own purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So it was -- but you would agree with me that it was a question of -- a question between the two parties, between the SDA and the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No. That was an issue between the administration and the SDS. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 17336 to 17342.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. At the same time that you were living in the municipality during this time, you became aware -- you became aware of the fact that there was a dispute by the Serbian members of the police department, and they moved into a station in Jasenica for a week. You remember that happening, do you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: At that time I lived in the municipality, and I remember that a Serb policeman split and went to Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And do you remember their rationale, that is, why the Serbian police split and moved into Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Is that a question that derives from my statement? If so, could you tell me the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't know if it's in your statement. I'd be glad to point to you where you talk about that. But I'm basically what I'm trying to do is to get you to tell me what your recollection of those events are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Cunningham --

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop for the break here, because we have overstepped by five minutes. In the meantime, the witness will have more time to go through his statement again. We will reconvene at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry for the delay, but we were engaged in some discussions in my chambers on a draft decision, and we needed to conclude. So Mr. Brdjanin is here. Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Before the break we talked briefly about the Branko Copic monument, and you told us that that was an issue between the administration and the SDS. And then I shifted topics to talk to you about the time when Serbian police officers moved for a period of time to a station in Jasenica. And you asked me if that was in your statement, and over the lunch hour -- excuse me, over the break I looked at the statement and didn't find a reference to it. Did you happen to find a reference to it in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No, there is no mention of it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Then what I would like for you to do is to go on your recollection, your memory of those events. You remember it happening. I think you just told us that. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Right. But could you give me the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think this happened sometime in 1991, I want to say April of 1991.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I know that it happened, but I cannot remember when it was exactly. Because there were many things happening at the time, and I suppose you do understand that, because there was a war in the neighbouring Croatia, and that particular event, I can say I remember it taking place, but I expect you will ask me some further questions regarding the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like to. And if you remember, fine; and if you don't remember, just tell me. It's okay. Do you remember, have any recollection of why it is that the Serb officers left and were gone for a week to another police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, listen, the SDS submitted to us officially, I mean to the administrative bodies of the municipality, a draft, a project of the separation of the splitting away of the Serb municipality, and I knew that some citizens, because these kind of stories went around the town, that they had set up their own assembly, that they had taken certain decisions that even factories and businesses would be taken out. And they were simply engaged in taking out that part of the municipality, even though they continued working for the municipal agencies, even though they held various offices there. But at the same time, they were engaged in separating the Serb municipality. And perhaps this was part of it, because the police is an important segment of life in any municipality. And I suppose that was a kind of a trial run, to see if they could do it and if that segment could be made operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: What I would like for you to do is I'd like for you to tell us, if you know the answer, to tell us the answer, but I don't want you to speculate as to what that answer might be. Do you know - yes or no - why it is that the Serb police officers left and went to Jasenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, not specifically. I think this was to serve as a kind of a trial, as a kind of a test.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, you don't really know that. That's just your guess, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, look. We had -- but this is quite a long story, and I don't know. But we had problems with the weapons of the TO, with the transfer of the TO into the reserve police force, and then the distribution of the weaponry there. So perhaps that could be one of the reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think in all fairness, we have to distinguish two parts of his answer. There is one part where I agree with you, Mr. Cunningham, that there is an element of personal opinion, speculation. There is the other part, however, which -- in which he's quite categoric, in which he says the SDS submitted to them officially, I mean to the administrative bodies of the municipality, a draft, a project of the separation of the splitting away of the Serbian municipality. So in that, he's not speculating. He's giving us a fact. So for the record, we keep the two things separate.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: You would agree with me that when the Serbs -- the Serb police officers left the police department and went off on their own for that one-week period, do you think that that was a political decision made by the SDS? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: They quit. I don't know about the time, but that was a political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And just like the dispute over Branko Copic, the monument, it appeared to you, from your position, that this police department split, was a political decision made by the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Branko Copic has nothing to do with the police. Branko Copic, it was the issue which had to do with the relations between the administration and the SDS, because the decision to put up this monument was unlawful, and the police was part of their idea to separate, to take out the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Because you cannot partition the municipality without solving the question of the police at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And you know from your position that the Serbian officers came back and returned to the main police station in Bosanska Krupa; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Try -- first of all, we need to redact this last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Secondly, Witness, try -- when you are about to tell us something that could reveal your identity, just ask me to go into private session. Then you are free to say what you like, because no one else will hear you. But if you give us information like you did, and there are others listening, they will immediately know who you are, in spite of the fact that we took precautions to hide your identity. All right? So Madam Chuqing, please provide for the redaction. Mr. Cunningham, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, maybe it would be best if I asked a couple of questions in private session first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's go into private session for a while, and you can repeat the question actually as well, so he can answer it in private session

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I want to talk to you about someone that you came to know during your time in Bosanska Krupa, and that is Mr. Klickovic. And you know who I'm talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Some people have described him as being arrogant. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: He had a loud voice.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. How would you describe him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: He had a loud voice. He had a big moustache. He had a certain look, a specific look.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this: In your time in your municipality, you had several dealings with him; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: We very often went to Sarajevo together to carry out some projects that had to do with the road infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And particularly, in the week before the attack on Bosanska Krupa, you had the opportunity to meet with him on several occasions? And again, I don't want you to reveal what your position was. I just want to confirm with you that you had discussions and meetings with Mr. Klickovic in the week before the assault on Bosanska Krupa; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, as he was employed in the municipality, we worked in the same building, so I could speak to him every day if it was necessary. And even before the attack, we would meet and speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Specifically, before the attack, there were meetings between the local politicians in control and the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: We were all local politicians and the SDS, just like the SDA, was also in power.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And one of the things that you were trying to do was trying to find a peaceful resolution to the situation in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to find that kind of a solution. Perhaps I even wanted such a solution desperately, because I was aware of the danger facing my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And in trying to find that peaceful solution, you spoke with Mr. Klickovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes. On the whole, we spoke about dividing the municipality into a Serbian part and into another part, because they persisted in requesting such a partition.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. Based on your discussions with Mr. Klickovic, do you feel he is the -- is he the sort of person who would tell you one thing and do another thing? Is he someone you considered to be truthful and honest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Before he assumed power, he had a bad background. He had been in prison for certain reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. But based on your dealings with him, especially in that last week, do you feel he dealt with you in a truthful and honest fashion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: When the knife is suspended above your neck, it's difficult for you to assess such things.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, looking back, do you feel like -- looking back now, do you feel like he dealt with you honestly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: We watched the Croatian television broadcast, or rather, it was a Montenegrin television, together in my office. We watched them showing the shelling of Dubrovnik from a position that was held by the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, and the person firing from a gun at Dubrovnik, his main problem was to avoid the barrel of the gun from overheating. He fired at a cultural monument. I asked Gojko what he thought about this, and at that point he told me that this was a legitimate target, that in fact it was war booty. I was surprised. I was nonplussed by such an answer, and you can imagine the opinion I had of him at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: So let me ask my question again, and if you can answer it, fine; and if you can't, that's okay too. Looking back, do you consider him to be an honest person, someone that you would trust? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I can't trust him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your statements, you talk about Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. You didn't trust him then, and you are happy today that you never trusted him then? Is that the substance, the essence of your answer? Did you trust him at any time during these negotiations 11 years ago or 12 years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believed in the possibility of finding a solution. He was a legitimate person with whom to negotiate, and I believed that it was possible to find a solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But did you trust him? And if you trusted him at any point in time, did you continue trusting him or did you lose confidence in him, trust in him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by what I said. I said it was legitimate to negotiate with him. I believed that it was possible to find a solution. If he had wanted to find a solution, a solution would have been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: In your statement, and I want you to confirm this, you say: "Gojko Klickovic appeared to be the coordinator for SDS activities in the area of Bosanska Krupa." Do you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. In this case, you also gave a statement on 31 March 1998 to the -- in Bihac to the people from AID. Do you remember giving a statement to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I remember that they contacted me and that I gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And did you -- have you had the opportunity to look at that statement since you have been here in the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't know if that statement has been made available to him, but I'd ask that the B/C/S version be made available to the witness. He has it? I'm sorry. I didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, we will provide a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I think he already has it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please check. This is the statement that was given by the witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- on the 31st of March of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We just provided a copy, because we didn't tender that statement into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the understanding, that it's not been tendered, no. Yes, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And again, I'm going to just ask you to confirm a couple of statements that are in here. In the English language version of this, and I realise it's probably no help to you, but on page 2, very near the bottom, is this statement, and this is given, just so that you understand the context of this statement, in the AID statement you have just described how Mr. Martic was released, that you are driving back to Bosanska Krupa, and you're talking about how, on the way back to Bosanska Krupa, you and Mr. Klickovic and another gentleman are telling the Serbs at the checkpoints to go home; there's no need to be out. And in the statement, you ask -- it says as follows: "I asked Klickovic how many soldiers do you have here? He answered: Around 5.000. Then I could see for myself that Klickovic was very influential and he has command over armed men." Did you see that portion in your statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And I apologise for interrupting. And you still confirm that today; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes, I stand by this claim.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: And on the very next page, about midway down the page on page 3 in the English version is the following passage, and I'm going to read it slow so that it can be translated. You say: "It can definitely be said that the key people of the Bosanska Krupa SDS, the be-all and end-all of all activities that took place, then and later, were Miroslav Vjestica and Gojko Klickovic, as organisers and order-issuing authorities, they bear more responsibility than anyone else." Do you still stand by that position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: There's one final area that I want to go to, and it requires us to go back to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'd just go back to Exhibit 1649. That is the exhibit that you read for the first time yesterday. To refresh your recollection it is the document that you believe was authored by Mr. Klickovic. And I want to take you on the -- to the English version on page 4. And I apologise for not being able to point you to the exact passage, but it is a paragraph that begins with the phrase: "The negotiations began on 16 January 1992 and gave no promise of a peaceful outcome." That's the very first sentence in the paragraph. I don't know if --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry. In B/C/S, it is page 2, last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I would like for you to go --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I would like for you to go down about halfway through the paragraph, and I'm going to read slow to see if you can find this passage: "This was the time when the Serbian people were saved and the Serbian territory preserved. This is a report on their work and the protagonists were Serbs." Do you see where that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I do

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: "Members of the SDS. So here we will mention just a few of them." And what follows is one, two, three, four, five, six people who are mentioned specifically; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Nowhere in those lists of six people do we see the defendant's name, do we, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: The authors always forget to put their names in.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Well, no. Here's my question: You told us that the -- you believed that the author was Mr. Klickovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My question to you is: We don't see Mr. Brdjanin's name there at all, do we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No, we don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I'd like you to go to the next page -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Ms. Richterova, if you can help me. I'm talking about now page 5 of the English version, the very first paragraph at the top, the very last sentence. So if -- with the Court's permission, she could help the witness get situated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me how the paragraph starts?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If you go to page 5 of the English version, it is the first -- it starts: "Of the P/illegible area to the right bank of the Una."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To help you, Ms. Richterova, the next paragraph starts: "The primary and basic role of the War Presidency."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was the easier way to do it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It should be page 4 in B/C/S, first full paragraph, somewhere in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: If you can find the paragraph that begins: "The primary and basic role," Mr. Witness. What I'm going to ask you to do is find that and then look up one sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Have you found that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I have page 4, and the first paragraph says: "The War Presidency made an assessment of the situation and took the only proper, correct decision."

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Look up one more paragraph. Go up one paragraph and then go up one more sentence, so that the very last sentence in -- so that the very last sentence in the paragraph I'm asking you to read says: "This presidency took all crucial military and civilian decisions." Do you see that sentence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: "The primary and basic task of the War Presidency was to liberate all areas on the right bank of the Una, making --"

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Let me stop you there, and I don't do that to be disrespectful to you. But do you see that the very sentence before that, up one paragraph -- can you find that sentence and read it? It starts with the words: "This War Presidency" or "The War Presidency." Excuse me. It starts out with simply: "This presidency ..."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Right. Just go on asking. I'm sure it exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Okay. And you would agree with me that Klickovic was the sort of person that could make those sorts of decisions, was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: May I have just a minute, Your Honour? Because I think I'm almost done. That's all I have, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. Madam Richterova, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour. There is no re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Janu? Sir, Judge Janu from the Czech Republic has got a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, when describing your experience from media with Mr. Brdjanin, you said few, few things. You said that you saw him at least 20 times on television. You said that he acted authoritatively, or in authoritative manner. You also said that he was obviously an important man. And you also said that people would turn to him with regard to many issues. And you, when asked by the Defence counsel, you said that you don't remember what he said, any quotes. My question is: Can you recall what was the spirit of his presentation, I mean the way how he presented his arguments?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: If you mean the overall impression, I've already said it when I said that he had this authoritative approach. And if you mean the substance of his speeches, well, that was the SDS policy, which I could recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And would you classify him, or the way he speaks, as -- would you classify him as a powerful speaker, powerful orator, who can catch the people's attention easily?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: By all means, because I don't know which rank he held in the SDS, but I know that he could pull a lot of weight.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second area of questioning is concerning the communistic past of your country. Am I right that you were not a member of the Communist Party, of the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: No, you're not right. I was a member of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: And my second question in this field: In your opinion, did the political system during the era of Marshal Tito, and later on, until 1990, display the basic democratic features?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: It tried to rectify the situation, largely under the influence of Slovenian -- of the Slovenian policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: No, I don't think you caught my point. I was asking if it's your opinion that the previous system, political system, displayed a basic democratic features.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: It was a single-party system, but within it, one could live. It wasn't repressive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: In your opinion, did this system contribute to the atrocities and the situation, whole situation in your country after 1990?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, yes, because it had failed it resolve some fundamental issues concerning the relations between and among the republics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: That's only what you can think about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: I think that this -- that is all that is needed at this point, because if we go into it, then it will take some time to tell the whole story. Then I will have to speak from the point of view of the people that I belonged to and accuse that system of the victims of this war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have just one simple question to you. You've told us, and you've repeated, that you actually, during the time of 1992, 1991/1992, that you saw the accused Brdjanin on TV some -- more than 20 times. Compared to other politicians of the same standing that he had, would you say that was average, less, than the appearances of others, or more? How did it feature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS BT96
utterances.text: Well, Krajisnik appeared more often. That is certain. Because he was the president of the Assembly. But Mr. Brdjanin was also frequently present in the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That brings us to the end of your testimony in this case. On behalf of Judge Janu, Judge Taya, myself, and also on behalf of the Tribunal in general, I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence. You will be attended to in order that you can return to your country of residence. And before you leave this courtroom, may I, on behalf of everyone, wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland, your presence here, I would assume, tells us that the next witness is already in line.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That's why my presence is here, but the witness is not ready, Your Honour, because of developments this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I expected it. Will he be ready, say --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He has a number of statements to read. He came over at 10.30 this morning, as soon as I became aware of the developments. So I contacted the VWU to have him brought here. I asked to be sent an e-mail to the courtroom when he had finished reading his statements, because there is a number of things I need to clarify with him. So I will need at least half an hour, three quarters of an hour to speak with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: But at this moment I haven't been advised that he's actually finished reading his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be in our -- I think we can safely break here now. We will be in our chambers, respective chambers. Will you let us know through the registrar, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So we will resume when we are in a position to resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. I understand you have encountered a problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, and I apologise for keeping all the parties waiting, but I was advised at 1.00 that the witness had just finished reading his statements. And even if I was to go upstairs and speak to the witness immediately, I would need a certain amounts of time to explain the court procedures and the protective measures involved, and I also needed to clarify one or two matters. So that would have taken at least half an hour to do that. So I don't think we should -- that there's any chance starting --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That will take us beyond our time limit in any case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So there is no problem this time, because perfectly I understand that there is a problem and that there's no sense in trying to approach it in any other manner. However, may I ask you: When did the witness arrive here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: He arrived not yesterday but the day before, and had I -- had I known what was going to develop this morning, then I could have spoken to the witness or brought the witness over yesterday afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber accepts that explanation. So we will need to adjourn today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: We are trying to bring the witnesses forward; however --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is what I was going to suggest, that all that is happening now was unexpected, could not have been anticipated, and one can understand, of course, that problems can arise. On the other hand, we are going to adopt the system that we adopted today. Perhaps you should keep in mind - when I say you, it's the whole team - two things in particular, two objectives. Number one is: To try and avoid as much as possible for the Tribunal to have witnesses stay here over the weekend unnecessarily, if that can be avoided, because it involves the Tribunal in additional expenses which I'm sure can be averted, can be avoided. And number two is: As you go along, try to liaise as much as possible with the Defence so that they are put in a position where they can catch up with the rhythm that we will be adopting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, two things. Firstly, in relation to trying to finish the witnesses as quickly as we can, with this next witness, BT56, I intend taking him through -- leading him through his evidence, because this is a very important witness in that it goes directly to the torture counts in the indictment. And so I do not propose tendering his statement at all, and that is in relation to the next witness only, that I can speak of. The other matter was: We were going to try and move all the witnesses up so that we do not have any lag in trial time in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can be planned.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: That may mean the witnesses may be here over the weekend, you know, if we don't get to their testimony. We're trying to bring up the witness that is required for cross-examination, the one that's scheduled at the moment for next Monday. We were trying to bring him here for this Friday, but that's not possible. I've been advised by the VWU.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that, Ms. Sutherland. I do not expect miracles. On the other hand, what I can tell you is this: That I could work out myself a schedule that I could impose, but I neither would like or should like to impose a schedule. I much rather prefer that you have a time limit and that you work within the parameters of that time limit without feeling any further restrictions or limitations than that. But on the other hand, if you do the same exercise that I have done, looking at the statements and distinguishing which witnesses can be just faced with the statement and which others need to be examined in more detail, believe me, it's quite possible to schedule the arrival of witnesses with any lapse of a weekend in between, with the exception of one witness, with the exception of one witness. And just for the record, the two expert witnesses that you have, without the need of us mentioning the names, you will -- the Chamber will exercise its discretion and limit the time that they will spend in this courtroom, both one and the other. And for that purpose, we will be limiting the time which you will have, as Prosecution, for the examination-in-chief. And the rest of the time will be devoted to the cross-examination. The reason for that is that there is the statement, or the report, of the expert witness in each case, in either case, and in both cases they are thorough reports. So I think we'll need to adjourn for today.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's just one other matter, in relation to the scheduling and finishing the Prosecution case by the 1st of August. One of the experts cannot testify before the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my problem, Ms. Sutherland. It's not my problem. I find it difficult to find how this person can find it impossible to come here for one day between now and the 1st day of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, apparently, I've been advised that she has already booked a holiday from mid-July and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Too bad.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And her statement has yet to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Too bad, Ms. Sutherland. Too bad. If you want her, bring her over. It's very easy for someone to miss a week or two and have to come here and do work and testify. It's no problem. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you find yourself in some other kind of difficulty, do come back to me, but certainly not that she will be inconvenienced if she comes over because she has booked her holiday. The case has to be over as far as the Prosecution is concerned by the 1st of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I add that her statement has yet to be finalised therefore it hasn't yet been disclosed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not my problem. You've had a year and a half to commission the expert on propaganda to finalise the statement and bring it forward. And now you have only got until the 1st of August. We stand adjourned. Tomorrow at 9.00. If possible, please liaise with the Defence to see whether Mr. Sebire is coming over tomorrow or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 12th day of June 2003, at 9.00 a.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.25 p.m.,
